The Story of Lubdhak the Merchant

I bow to Lord Jina, adorned with the splendour of omniscience and guru of the three worlds, and I write the story of Lubdhak the merchant.

Abhayvahan was king of Champapuri. His queen was Pundarika, whose eyes were like lotus blossoms. In Champapuri lived a merchant named Lubdhak, whose wife was Nagvasu. Lubdhak had two sons, Garuddatt and Nagdatt, both cheerful and good-natured.

Lubdhak was immensely wealthy. He had spent enormous sums to have pairs of every animal fashioned in solid gold — yaksha, birds, elephants, camels, horses, lions, deer, and more. Their horns, tails, and hooves were studded with precious diamonds, pearls, and gems, creating a dazzling display that astonished all who beheld it. Everyone who saw this glittering exhibition praised Lubdhak lavishly, and Lubdhak himself felt greatly fortunate as he gazed upon his shining collection.

Yet Lubdhak had one small sorrow: he had begun making a pair of golden bulls and had completed only one. The second bull could not be made because he had run out of gold. This alone troubled him — not any spiritual lack, not any moral failing, but simply the incompleteness of his collection. Rather than resting in contentment, he busied himself constantly trying to remedy this deficiency.

Once, rain fell continuously for seven days. Rivers and streams were all in flood. Yet the indomitable Lubdhak went to the river himself to gather wood for the second bull. He waded into the raging torrent, pulled out great bundles of timber, tied them up, and carried the heavy load on his own head back home. Truly, when has the thirst of such greedy men ever been quenched? Never.

At that time Queen Pundarika was sitting in her palace, admiring the beauty of nature. King Abhayvahan was there too. Seeing Lubdhak trudging along with an enormous bundle of firewood on his head, the queen said to the king, "My lord, it seems there is someone very poor in your kingdom. Look how that wretched man carries such a heavy load of wood on his head. Please show mercy and give him some help to ease his suffering." The compassionate are ever moved to help others.

The king at once sent servants to summon Lubdhak. When the merchant arrived, the king asked, "Are you in need? Do you require help?" Lubdhak was astonished and replied, "Maharaj, I am the wealthiest merchant in the city. I own property worth many crores. I carry this wood because I need it for my golden bull — not because I am poor." The king and queen were speechless. Here was a man richer than most kings, yet he risked his life in a flood for a piece of wood to complete a golden toy.

This story teaches that greed is an insatiable fire. Lubdhak had everything a person could desire — yet a single missing golden bull consumed his thoughts and drove him to risk his life in a raging flood. Those who possess much but desire more are poorer than those who possess little and are content. True wealth is not measured by gold and gems but by the peace of a satisfied heart.
